papers.full_text: AbstractWe report a case of prolonged active SARS-CoV-2 infection in a patient with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) receiving venetoclax. The patient demonstrated persistent symptoms over a span of 105 days and repeatedly positive SARS-CoV-2 polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing. The case highlights the diagnostic and therapeutic challenges in immunocompromised hosts, including limited guidance and drug availability. Management required multiple antiviral regimens and consideration of alternative therapies. This case underscores the need for further research that can inform more robust guidelines and therapeutic strategies in this vulnerable population.Keywords: sars-cov-2 in malignancy, sars-cov-2 prolonged active infection, sars-cov-2 (severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus-2), sars-cov-2 testing, sars-cov-2 treatment DiscussionProlonged SARS-CoV-2 infection is a rare and challenging entity, typically limited to severely immunocompromised patients. In these cases, viral clearance may be significantly delayed due to an impaired ability to mount an effective immune response. As a result, these patients may experience a relapsing or persistent clinical course marked by intermittent symptom flares and ongoing radiographic abnormalities [1,2,4,7,8]. It should be noted, however, that there is no universally accepted definition and timeline for what constitutes a prolonged active SARS-CoV-2 infection at this time, and standardization may be helpful in future research on the topic.Treatment strategies remain unstandardized, though emerging data support the use of extended course or combination antiviral therapy and monoclonal antibodies when available with favorable outcomes [3,5,8-11]. In the case presented, the patient required multiple rounds of antiviral therapy, including an extended course, and a prolonged clinical observation period. While high-titer convalescent plasma was considered [2] due to the inaccessibility of monoclonal antibodies and clinical improvement, this was not required.Ct values from PCR testing [3] were also used to help guide clinical decision-making and assess for active viral replication. While not routinely used in immunocompetent individuals, lower Ct values may indicate higher viral loads and active infection, especially in symptomatic immunocompromised patients. In this case, a Ct value of 30.2 with continued symptoms suggested ongoing active viral presence and supported the decision to continue therapy. Although Ct is not recommended for therapeutic monitoring [3], it may provide additional context in prolonged infections where symptom resolution, imaging, and virology may not agree.Prolonged SARS-CoV-2 infection is typically limited to severely immunocompromised patients. Treatment strategies remain unstandardized, though current available literature, composed of case reports and expert consensus, overall supports the use of dual antiviral therapy [8] and monoclonal antibodies [6] when available [3,4,10]. Due to limited access to monoclonals, convalescent plasma was considered in this case. Convalescent plasma would have served as an alternative to monoclonal antibodies given the concept of antibodies against the virus being present [6,7,11,12].Several limitations of this report warrant acknowledgment. Definitive distinction between persistent infection and reinfection cannot be established, as viral genomic sequencing, SARS-CoV-2 culture, and subgenomic RNA assays were not performed due in part to resource limitations. This challenge is further compounded by the absence of a universally accepted definition of prolonged active SARS-CoV-2 infection, meaning no formal diagnostic criteria exist against which this case can be adjudicated. The argument for persistence over reinfection rests on a convergence of laboratory, radiographic, and clinical findings, most notably among these being continuously unresolved respiratory symptoms, a consistent and progressing radiographic pattern, clinical deterioration temporally linked to procedural stress, laboratory values suggesting subclinical immune activation in the interval period, and attenuated humoral immunity evidenced by a low-magnitude spike antibody response despite full vaccination. Individually, none of these findings is definitive, but collectively they are believed to support this interpretation. However, even in the case of reinfection after cardiac catheterization, total illness duration would exceed 90 days, representing a significantly prolonged course of illness. Additional limitations include the absence of a Ct value at initial diagnosis, the inability of the multiplex respiratory panel used on Day 32 to report Cts, the unavailability of the antigen assay manufacturer and home test brand, and the lack of immunoglobulin level measurement during the clinical course. Despite the limitations, this case adequately emphasizes the need for individualized care and flexibility in therapeutic planning, particularly with respect to drug-drug interactions such as the CYP3A4 inhibition exhibited by ritonavir, which increases venetoclax plasma exposure and necessitated repeated interruption of CLL-directed therapy [4]. The balance between managing immunosuppression and facilitating viral clearance further highlights the importance of interdisciplinary coordination in such cases. ConclusionsThis case underscores three core learning points for clinicians managing SARS-CoV-2 in patients with hematologic malignancies. First, the combination of CLL-associated immune dysfunction and venetoclax-mediated B-cell suppression represents a uniquely high-risk for prolonged viral persistence, warranting heightened vigilance even when initial clinical improvement is observed. Second, the CYP3A4 inhibitory properties of ritonavir necessitate repeated interruption of venetoclax during nirmatrelvir/ritonavir courses, requiring proactive interdisciplinary coordination. Third, the absence of evidence-based guidelines for this population means management must be individualized, iterative, and informed by the best available evidence and resources at a given institution while acknowledging its limitations. Prospective research and standardized diagnostic frameworks for prolonged SARS-CoV-2 infection in immunocompromised patients remain an urgent need. IntroductionThe emergence of SARS-CoV-2 and the resulting global pandemic, lasting from December of 2019 to May of 2023, has highlighted both the adaptability of the virus and the vulnerability of certain patient populations. Among these, individuals who are immunocompromised, such as those receiving chemotherapy, biologic therapies, or immunosuppressive agents [1], face particularly complex challenges in the diagnosis, treatment, and clearance of the virus. In these patients, viral persistence rather than a short-lived acute illness can result [1-4].Prolonged or relapsing SARS-CoV-2 infection has been increasingly recognized in the literature [1-4] as a rare yet serious condition occurring in immunocompromised hosts. While no universally accepted definition currently exists, persistent SARS-CoV-2 infection has been broadly characterized as continued polymerase chain reaction (PCR) positivity with compatible symptoms lasting beyond 21 to 30 days in the setting of significant immunosuppression [3]. These cases often lack the typical immune-assisted viral clearance [2,5,6], resulting in extended periods of viral shedding and potential for progressive disease. The clinical approach to such patients is further complicated by the paucity of evidence-based guidelines, the evolving landscape of antiviral and monoclonal antibody therapies, and the consideration of drug interactions and immune modulation [4].Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is an indolent B-cell lymphoproliferative malignancy associated with well-characterized immune dysfunction affecting both humoral and cellular compartments. The malignant B-cell clone disrupts normal immune architecture, contributing to hypogammaglobulinemia and impaired T-cell function that collectively reduce the host's capacity for effective antiviral response [5]. Venetoclax, a selective BCL-2 inhibitor used in the treatment of CLL, further compounds this immune deficit by promoting apoptosis of BCL-2-overexpressing B cells, thereby impairing the generation of antigen-specific antibody responses necessary for viral clearance [4,5]. The convergence of these two mechanisms, CLL-associated immune dysregulation and venetoclax-mediated B-cell suppression, creates a permissive environment for prolonged viral persistence, providing distinction in this patient population from other immunocompromised hosts.This report discusses the prolonged course of SARS-CoV-2 in a patient with CLL receiving venetoclax, a BCL-2 inhibitor, and the evolving therapeutic decisions and clinical monitoring strategy utilized during their 105-day illness. By presenting the complex clinical decision-making and evolving response to treatment alongside the immunological context underlying this patient's vulnerability, we aim to contribute to the growing understanding of SARS-CoV-2 in immunocompromised patients. Case presentationA 69-year-old male with active CLL and 11q deletion, diagnosed over three years prior, on a stable dose of venetoclax, presented initially in January 2024, approximately six months after the end of the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, with a productive cough and sore throat. He had completed the primary SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccination series (Pfizer Inc., New York, NY, USA, and BioNTech SE, Mainz, Germany) with three additional boosters. At initial presentation (Day 0), he was hemodynamically stable with a SpO2 of 99% on room air and a mildly reduced tympanic temperature of 35.8°C (Table 1, Figure 1). He was diagnosed with SARS-CoV-2 via antigen testing. A confirmatory nucleic acid amplification test was not performed at the time of initial diagnosis, and no cycle threshold (Ct) value was therefore obtainable at disease onset.Table 1Patient's vital signs at the time of presentation.Demonstrating hemodynamic stability and a mildly reduced temperature not meeting the criteria for hypothermia (<35 degrees C).C: CelsiusVital SignsMeasurementUnitsBlood Pressure133 / 67mmHgHeart Rate68per minuteRespiratory Rate18per minuteSpO2 99%Tympanic Temperature35.8CFigure 1Detailed timeline from first positive SARS-CoV-2 test covering emergency department visits, hospital admissions, clinic visits, medication changes, imaging, pertinent temporal labs, and SARS-CoV-2 testing with final negative result.Red text: viral testing; blue text: antiviral therapies; brown text: chemotherapeutics; green text: radiographic imaging.GGOs: ground-glass opacities; CXR: chest X-ray; Ct: cycle threshold; IL-2α: interleukin 2-alpha; elev.: elevated/elevation; (+): positive result; (-): negative result; PET-CT: positron emission tomography- computed tomography; BAL: bronchoalveolar lavage; ESR: erythrocyte sedimentation rate; CRP: C-reactive protein; CTPA: computed tomography pulmonary angiography; LUL: left upper lobe; RLL: right lower lobe; DC: discontinue(d)Image credits: Authors, using Miro (RealtimeBoard, Inc.), San Francisco, CA, USA.He completed a five-day course of nirmatrelvir/ritonavir (Paxlovid) beginning Day 10, with temporary cessation of venetoclax due to the CYP3A4 inhibitory effect of ritonavir and concern for increased venetoclax plasma exposure. Venetoclax was restarted on Day 16 at an oncology follow-up visit, the day after completion of the antiviral course. On Day 9, he presented to the emergency department with shortness of breath and underwent CT pulmonary angiography, which demonstrated multifocal multilobar ground-glass opacities without pulmonary embolism (Video 1). At that visit, laboratory evaluation revealed a mildly decreased white blood cell count, a normal absolute neutrophil count, and a low absolute lymphocyte count reflecting venetoclax-mediated B-cell suppression. Hepatic enzymes were mildly elevated, representing values present at baseline prior to this illness. Procalcitonin was 0.28 ng/mL (reference ≤0.5 ng/mL), arguing against a primary bacterial process (Table 2).Table 2Relevant lab testing that occurred over the entire clinical course of the case. Trends notable and supportive of SARS-CoV-2 infection include (A) white blood cell (WBC) counts that show an initial mild leukopenia with a rise and subsequent fall with resolution of infection, never exceeding the upper limit of normal. (B) Absolute neutrophil and (C) absolute lymphocyte counts remain within normal limits despite active infection, consistent with immunosuppression. (D) Liver enzymes showed initial mild elevations with resolution toward the end of the clinical course, and (E) inflammatory markers support the active inflammatory process of infection. (F) Procalcitonin at the initial emergency department visit indicated a lower likelihood of bacterial infection at that time. On dates in which (G) cycle thresholds were obtained with PCR testing, they were also noted and showed no consistent trend; however, they are indicative of COVID positivity and support the presence of infection without signs of increased viral burden rather than improvement before the final testing, at which point the cycle threshold was not achieved to indicate the presence of infection. Following completion of the antiviral course, the patient reported two negative home rapid antigen tests within the two days prior to Day 18 and overall improvement in symptoms, though residual cough with white phlegm persisted. During the hospital course, the patient required supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula in the setting of fever and worsening respiratory status, with documented oxygen saturation of 94% on 2 liters via nasal cannula during an overnight rapid response event on Day 34. papers.full_text_excerpt: As a result, these patients may experience a relapsing or persistent clinical course marked by intermittent symptom flares and ongoing radiographic abnormalities [1,2,4,7,8]. The argument for persistence over reinfection rests on a convergence of laboratory, radiographic, and clinical findings, most notably among these being continuously unresolved respiratory symptoms, a consistent and progressing radiographic pattern, clinical deterioration temporally linked to procedural stress, laboratory values suggesting subclinical immune activation in the interval period, and attenuated humoral immunity evidenced by a low-magnitude spike antibody response despite full vaccination. Individually, none of these findings is definitive, but collectively they are believed to support this interpretation. In these patients, viral persistence rather than a short-lived acute illness can result [1-4].Prolonged or relapsing SARS-CoV-2 infection has been increasingly recognized in the literature [1-4] as a rare yet serious condition occurring in immunocompromised hosts. AbstractWe report a case of prolonged active SARS-CoV-2 infection in a patient with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) receiving venetoclax. The patient demonstrated persistent symptoms over a span of 105 days and repeatedly positive SARS-CoV-2 polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing. The case highlights the diagnostic and therapeutic challenges in immunocompromised hosts, including limited guidance and drug availability. Management required multiple antiviral regimens and consideration of alternative therapies. papers.title_original: Prolonged Active SARS-CoV-2 Infection in a Patient With Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia on Venetoclax

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to highlight the diagnostic and therapeutic challenges of prolonged SARS-CoV-2 infection in immunocompromised patients, particularly those with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) on venetoclax. This is a rare and challenging entity, typically limited to severely immunocompromised patients.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This case study describes a single patient with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) receiving venetoclax who experienced prolonged active SARS-CoV-2 infection. The patient demonstrated persistent symptoms over a span of 105 days and repeatedly positive SARS-CoV-2 polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing.
analysis.methods: The patient's management involved multiple antiviral regimens and consideration of alternative therapies. Ct values from PCR testing were used to guide clinical decision-making and assess for active viral replication. High-titer convalescent plasma was considered due to the inaccessibility of monoclonal antibodies and clinical improvement, though it was not required.
analysis.main_results: The patient had a Ct value of 30.2 with continued symptoms, indicating ongoing active viral presence. Persistent SARS-CoV-2 infection was characterized by continued PCR positivity with compatible symptoms lasting beyond 21 to 30 days in the setting of significant immunosuppression.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The case suggests that prolonged SARS-CoV-2 infection may be associated with an impaired immune response, leading to delayed viral clearance and a relapsing or persistent clinical course. The use of Ct values in assessing active viral replication may be particularly relevant in symptomatic immunocompromised patients.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings emphasize the need for individualized, iterative management strategies for prolonged SARS-CoV-2 infection in immunocompromised patients, especially those with hematologic malignancies. They also highlight the importance of developing standardized diagnostic frameworks for this condition.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on a single case, which limits the generalizability of the findings. However, the evidence is grounded in the patient's clinical course and PCR results, supporting a moderate confidence level in the interpretation of prolonged active SARS-CoV-2 infection in this specific population.

analysis.summary_en: This case study reports a prolonged active SARS-CoV-2 infection in a patient with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) receiving venetoclax. The patient exhibited persistent symptoms over 105 days and repeated positive PCR results, indicating ongoing viral replication. The case highlights the challenges of diagnosing and treating SARS-CoV-2 in immunocompromised individuals, particularly those with hematologic malignancies. The authors emphasize the need for individualized management strategies and standardized diagnostic frameworks for prolonged infection. The study also notes the importance of considering drug interactions, such as the CYP3A4 inhibitory properties of ritonavir, which may affect venetoclax therapy. While the evidence is based on a single case, it provides valuable insights into the unique risks and management considerations for this vulnerable population. The findings suggest that lower Ct values may indicate higher viral loads in symptomatic immunocompromised patients, supporting the use of extended antiviral therapy and monoclonal antibodies when available.

papers.full_text: BackgroundThe epidemiology of pediatric acute respiratory infections (ARIs) changed substantially during the COVID-19 (coronavirus disease 2019) pandemic, largely because of school closures, masking, reduced travel, and other non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs). However, hospital-based data from the restriction period remain useful for describing pathogen detection patterns, clinical severity, and markers of adverse clinical course.MethodsWe conducted a retrospective hospital-based study of 62 children aged <18 years who were evaluated for ARI symptoms and underwent real-time fluorescent quantitative nucleic acid testing for common respiratory pathogens, including respiratory viruses and Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Demographic, clinical, laboratory, treatment, severity, and outcome variables were extracted from medical records. Continuous variables were summarized using medians and ranges, and group comparisons used non-parametric tests. Given the small sample size and sparse severe-outcome events, the study was not powered to detect small effect sizes, and regression findings were interpreted conservatively as hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory.ResultsThe median age was 9 years (range, 1–17), and 33 patients (53.2%) were female. Most children had mild disease (37/62, 59.7%); 19 (30.6%) had moderate disease and 6 (9.7%) had severe disease. Intensive care unit (ICU) admission was recorded in 6 patients (9.7%), and mechanical ventilatory or noninvasive respiratory support in 9 (14.5%). Fever (43.5%) and cough (22.6%) were the most frequent presenting symptoms. Median oxygen saturation was 94.7% (range, 87.2–97.8). Respiratory virus detection was documented in 15 children (24.2%). Human rhinovirus was detected in 15 children (24.2%), human bocavirus in 9 (14.5%), and Mycoplasma pneumoniae in 10 (16.1%); co-detection was recorded in 14 children (22.6%). Lower SpO2 and longer symptom duration differed significantly across severity categories (both p < 0.001). In exploratory logistic regression, each additional day of symptoms was associated with higher odds of hospital admission/continued inpatient management [odds ratio [OR], 1.4; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.03–1.93; p = 0.022]. Sex was not significantly associated with clinical severity or laboratory parameters.ConclusionsIn this small hospital-based pediatric ARI cohort during the COVID-19 restriction period, severe disease was uncommon, and oxygen saturation and symptom duration were the most clinically coherent markers of greater severity. The observed pathogen detection pattern is compatible with pandemic-era disruption of respiratory pathogen circulation, but causal conclusions about NPIs require larger denominator-based studies with pre-pandemic and post-restriction comparison groups. 2Methods2.1Study design, setting, and reporting frameworkThis was a retrospective hospital-based observational study conducted in the Department of Pediatric Emergency at Shanxi Provincial Children's Hospital, Taiyuan, Shanxi Province, China. The study period extended from January 2020 to December 2021, corresponding to the COVID-19 restriction period in China. The manuscript was structured to align with the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) recommendations for reporting observational studies (13). Because the dataset included only children with ARI encounters and pathogen testing, the study should be interpreted as a clinical case-series/observational cohort rather than as a population prevalence study.2.2ParticipantsEligible participants were children aged <18 years with symptoms compatible with ARI, including fever, cough, sore throat, rhinorrhea, dyspnea, or shortness of breath, who underwent respiratory pathogen nucleic acid testing during the study period. A total of 96 children with ARI-compatible presentations were initially screened during 2020–2021. Exclusion criteria were: duplicate encounters for the same illness episode, incomplete core clinical records, or absence of respiratory pathogen test results. Applying these criteria led to exclusion of 34 children (12 duplicate encounters, 15 with incomplete core clinical records, and 7 without respiratory pathogen test results). The final analytic sample included 62 children. Because respiratory pathogen testing was ordered at the treating physician's discretion rather than through universal screening, children with more severe or prolonged symptoms may have been preferentially tested, and this selection pattern should be considered when interpreting pathogen-detection frequencies and their association with severity. The participant-selection process is summarized in the flow diagram (Figure 1).Figure 1Participant selection flow diagram showing the number of children screened for eligibility, excluded (with reasons), and included in the final analytic sample.Flowchart showing selection of children with acute respiratory infection-compatible presentations screened between 2020 and 2021, with n equal to ninety-six initially screened, thirty-four excluded for reasons listed, and sixty-two in the final analytic sample with respiratory pathogen testing.2.3Data collectionDemographic and clinical data were extracted from charts and electronic medical records by trained reviewers. Variables included age, sex, body weight, height, body mass index (BMI), symptom type and duration, oxygen saturation (SpO2), hospital admission/continued inpatient management, intensive care unit (ICU) admission, mechanical ventilation/noninvasive respiratory support, length of hospital and ICU stay, white blood cell count (WBC), C-reactive protein (CRP), procalcitonin, pathogen test results, co-detection, antiviral therapy, antibiotic therapy, corticosteroid use, supportive treatment, severity classification, and clinical outcome. Personal identifiers were coded before analysis.2.4Pathogen testingRespiratory specimens were tested using real-time fluorescent quantitative PCR (polymerase chain reaction) assays for common respiratory viruses and Mycoplasma pneumoniae RNA/DNA. Nasopharyngeal swab specimens were collected within 24 h of presentation and processed in the hospital's clinical microbiology laboratory using a multiplex respiratory pathogen panel targeting influenza A and B viruses, respiratory syncytial virus, human rhinovirus, human bocavirus, human metapneumovirus, parainfluenza viruses 1–3, adenovirus, seasonal coronaviruses, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Each assay run included a positive control, a negative (no-template) control, and an internal amplification control to monitor extraction and amplification efficiency, following the reagent manufacturer's instructions and routine laboratory quality-assurance procedures. A specimen was classified as positive for a given pathogen when the cycle-threshold value was below the manufacturer-specified cutoff with a typical sigmoidal amplification curve and a valid internal control; results with an invalid internal control or atypical amplification curve were repeated before being reported.2.5DefinitionsARI was defined clinically by compatible acute respiratory symptoms. Severity was categorized as mild, moderate, or severe. Co-detection was defined as detection of more than one respiratory pathogen in the same illness episode. Clinical outcome was categorized as recovery, complication, or death according to discharge records. Hospital admission/continued inpatient management was defined as continued observation and treatment beyond the initial emergency evaluation, consistent with the emergency-department-based case mix of this cohort, in which most children were evaluated, treated, and discharged without formal ward admission. Mechanical ventilatory/noninvasive respiratory support was recorded independently of formal admission status and could be provided during emergency-department management; therefore, the number of children receiving such support does not necessarily correspond to the number meeting admission criteria.2.6Ethical considerationsThe study was approved by the Ethics Committee. Because this was a retrospective analysis of de-identified records, the requirement for individual informed consent was waived.2.7Statistical analysisContinuous variables were summarized using medians and ranges because the distributions were non-normal and the sample was small. Categorical variables were summarized as frequencies and percentages. Sex-based and pathogen-detection group comparisons were performed using Mann–Whitney U tests for continuous variables and Fisher exact or chi-square tests for categorical variables as appropriate. Comparisons across severity categories used Kruskal–Wallis tests with post-hoc pairwise comparisons when the global test was significant. Binary logistic regression was used exploratorily to assess predictors of hospital admission/continued inpatient management. Ordinal logistic regression was used exploratorily for severity. Candidate predictors for the multivariable models (age, sex, weight, SpO2, and duration of symptoms) were selected a priori on the basis of clinical plausibility and were retained for multivariable modeling if they showed an association with the outcome at p < 0.20 in univariable analysis; because of the limited number of severe and admitted cases, each multivariable model was restricted to a maximum of two predictors to maintain an events-per-variable ratio of at least 3, and full model estimates with 95% confidence intervals for every predictor are reported in Table 1. Multicollinearity among candidate predictors was assessed using variance inflation factors, all of which were below 2.5, indicating no substantial collinearity. Because of sparse outcome cells, multinomial outcome regression was not retained as a primary inferential model; prognosis was interpreted descriptively. All p-values were two-sided, and p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Analyses were conducted using IBM SPSS Statistics version 27 (14). Oxygen supplementation was recorded in 7 children (11.3%), and intravenous fluids in 2 children (3.2%) (Figure 5). full_text_sections.discussion: 4DiscussionIn this retrospective hospital-based study of 62 children with ARIs evaluated during the COVID-19 restriction period, most cases were mild, severe disease was uncommon, and ICU admission occurred in fewer than 10% of children. The most coherent clinical severity markers were lower oxygen saturation and longer symptom duration. Respiratory virus detection was documented in approximately one quarter of children, with rhinovirus being the most frequently detected virus and Mycoplasma pneumoniae detected in a smaller but clinically relevant proportion. Co-detection occurred in more than one fifth of the cohort.The finding that low SpO2 tracked with disease severity is clinically expected and strengthens internal validity. Oxygen saturation is an objective bedside indicator of lower respiratory tract involvement and impaired gas exchange. This pattern is consistent with prior pediatric respiratory cohorts in which oxygen saturation and other clinical features tracked with severity, although such bedside features alone have limited ability to identify the causative pathogen (15). Similarly, longer symptom duration may indicate delayed presentation, progressive disease, treatment failure, or more persistent infection, explaining its association with admission/continued inpatient management. Comparable associations between prolonged symptom duration and hospital-based management have been reported in rhinovirus-associated pediatric acute respiratory infection (16). These findings support prioritizing oxygen saturation and symptom trajectory in triage and follow-up decisions for pediatric ARIs.The pathogen profile should be interpreted in the context of pandemic-era transmission disruption. Multiple studies from China and other settings have reported altered circulation, reduced activity, or delayed resurgence of several pediatric respiratory pathogens during and after COVID-19 restrictions. In mainland China, detection rates for common respiratory viruses declined during periods of strict NPIs and rebounded after restrictions were relaxed, with earlier and more pronounced rhinovirus and Mycoplasma pneumoniae activity reported in several post-restriction cohorts (5, 9, 10, 17–19). Comparable patterns of viral suppression followed by resurgence have also been described in Taiwan, Hong Kong, and other East Asian settings (6–8, 20). However, the present dataset cannot directly estimate the population prevalence of ARIs or quantify the independent effect of NPIs because it lacks a denominator, a pre-pandemic comparator group, and post-restriction follow-up. Therefore, the current results are best framed as a hospital-based description of ARI cases and pathogen detection during 2020–2021 rather than as evidence of NPI efficacy by themselves.The relative predominance of rhinovirus in this cohort is biologically plausible. As a non-enveloped virus, rhinovirus is comparatively resistant to environmental degradation and to some hygiene-based interventions that primarily disrupt transmission of enveloped viruses such as influenza and respiratory syncytial virus, which may explain its continued circulation when other pathogens were suppressed (3, 21). Co-detection of rhinovirus with other respiratory pathogens is also frequently reported in pediatric cohorts and does not necessarily indicate greater severity, consistent with the absence of a significant association between virus detection and severity category in the present data (16, 21–23). Mycoplasma pneumoniae follows a multi-year epidemic cycle of approximately 3–7 years that is thought to reflect population immunity dynamics rather than short-term public health measures; detection of Mycoplasma pneumoniae in this cohort during the restriction period is therefore compatible with its intrinsic epidemic periodicity rather than a specific NPI-related effect (5, 24–26).The high rate of antibiotic use deserves careful interpretation. Antibiotics were prescribed in three quarters of children despite respiratory virus detection in a minority and low median procalcitonin. This pattern may reflect empirical management during diagnostic uncertainty, concern for atypical pathogens such as Mycoplasma pneumoniae, local protocols, or severity-based treatment decisions. This proportion exceeds the confirmed bacterial or atypical-pathogen detection rate in this cohort and mirrors a broader pattern of empirical antibiotic use described in other pandemic-era pediatric respiratory cohorts (9, 19). Future studies should evaluate antimicrobial stewardship indicators, bacterial culture results, radiological findings, and outcomes to distinguish appropriate empirical therapy from potentially avoidable antibiotic exposure.The absence of significant sex-based differences suggests that sex was not a major determinant of laboratory findings or clinical course in this small cohort. Although the original ordinal model produced a numerically higher odds ratio for female sex, this was not statistically significant and should not be interpreted as evidence of sex-related severity differences. This null finding is consistent with most pediatric ARI cohorts, in which sex has not emerged as a consistent independent predictor of severity (24, 27). Broader demographic and clinical characteristics nonetheless remain relevant to the risk and clinical presentation of respiratory infections in paediatric patients (28).4.1Strengths and limitationsThis study provides real-world hospital-based data during a unique period of respiratory pathogen disruption. It includes demographic, clinical, laboratory, treatment, pathogen-detection, severity, and outcome data, allowing integrated description of clinical phenotype and severity markers.Important limitations must be acknowledged. First, the sample size was small, and only six severe cases were recorded; therefore, multivariable models are exploratory and at risk of overfitting. Second, the single-center retrospective design limits generalizability and may introduce selection, documentation, and testing biases, including selection bias from physician-discretion pathogen testing rather than universal screening, which may have enriched the tested sample for more symptomatic or severe presentations. Third, the dataset does not include a population denominator, pre-pandemic comparison group, or post-restriction group, preventing true prevalence estimation and causal inference about NPIs. Fourth, the dataset did not include SARS-CoV-2 co-testing status, a validated disease-severity scoring instrument, radiological findings, or blood culture results, which limits assessment of SARS-CoV-2 co-infection and of relative bacterial versus viral contributions to severity. Fifth, because hospital admission/continued inpatient management was defined broadly to include continued observation beyond initial emergency evaluation (Methods), the low proportion of children with formal ward admission reflects this definition and should not be read as indicating a non-hospital-based sample. Finally, sparse-outcome regression for prognosis produced unstable estimates and was not suitable for primary interpretation; future analyses of similarly small, sparse-event pediatric ARI datasets may benefit from penalized regression approaches, such as Firth's correction, to reduce small-sample bias (29). Because mechanical ventilatory/noninvasive respiratory support was captured as a separate variable from formal admission status, these counts should not be assumed to be nested, and readers should refer to the Definitions subsection when comparing the two.
full_text_sections.conclusion: 5ConclusionAmong children with ARIs evaluated during the COVID-19 restriction period, most cases were mild and severe disease was infrequent. Lower oxygen saturation and longer symptom duration were the most clinically meaningful markers of greater severity and admission/continued inpatient management. Respiratory virus detection, especially rhinovirus, and pathogen co-detection were observed, but the study should be interpreted as a hospital-based clinical description rather than a denominator-based prevalence analysis. Larger multicenter studies with pre-pandemic, restriction-period, and post-restriction comparison groups are needed to clarify the long-term effects of pandemic control measures on pediatric respiratory pathogen epidemiology and clinical outcomes.
full_text_sections.other: 1IntroductionAcute respiratory infections (ARIs) remain among the most frequent causes of pediatric illness, health-care use, antimicrobial exposure, and hospitalization worldwide (1). Their clinical spectrum ranges from self-limited upper respiratory tract infections to severe lower respiratory tract disease, respiratory failure, and death, particularly among young children, children with comorbidities, and populations with limited access to timely care (2).Pediatric ARIs are etiologically heterogeneous. Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), rhinovirus/enterovirus, influenza viruses, parainfluenza viruses, adenovirus, human metapneumovirus, human bocavirus, seasonal coronaviruses, atypical bacteria such as Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and bacterial pathogens may produce overlapping clinical syndromes (3, 4). Because fever, cough, dyspnea, and inflammatory markers are not sufficiently pathogen-specific, laboratory testing is often required to characterize etiology and guide infection-control and antimicrobial decisions (5).The COVID-19 pandemic created an unusual natural experiment in respiratory pathogen transmission. Non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs), including masking, hand hygiene, school closures, travel restrictions, isolation policies, and reduced social mixing, were associated in many settings with reduced circulation of several non-SARS-CoV-2 (severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2) respiratory viruses (6–8). Subsequent relaxation of restrictions was followed by altered seasonality and resurgence of pathogens such as RSV, influenza, rhinovirus, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae in several pediatric cohorts (9–11).For small hospital-based datasets collected during the restriction period, the strongest contribution is not estimation of population prevalence or causal attribution to NPIs, but careful description of clinical patterns, pathogen detection, and severity markers (12). Such data can help hospitals interpret pandemic-era case mix, identify simple bedside indicators of severity, and design larger surveillance studies.Therefore, this study aimed to describe the demographic, clinical, laboratory, treatment, and pathogen-detection characteristics of children evaluated for ARIs during 2020–2021, and to explore clinical markers associated with disease severity, hospital admission/continued inpatient management, and prognosis. 2.2ParticipantsEligible participants were children aged <18 years with symptoms compatible with ARI, including fever, cough, sore throat, rhinorrhea, dyspnea, or shortness of breath, who underwent respiratory pathogen nucleic acid testing during the study period. A total of 96 children with ARI-compatible presentations were initially screened during 2020–2021. Exclusion criteria were: duplicate encounters for the same illness episode, incomplete core clinical records, or absence of respiratory pathogen test results. Applying these criteria led to exclusion of 34 children (12 duplicate encounters, 15 with incomplete core clinical records, and 7 without respiratory pathogen test results). The final analytic sample included 62 children. Because respiratory pathogen testing was ordered at the treating physician's discretion rather than through universal screening, children with more severe or prolonged symptoms may have been preferentially tested, and this selection pattern should be considered when interpreting pathogen-detection frequencies and their association with severity. The participant-selection process is summarized in the flow diagram (Figure 1).Figure 1Participant selection flow diagram showing the number of children screened for eligibility, excluded (with reasons), and included in the final analytic sample.Flowchart showing selection of children with acute respiratory infection-compatible presentations screened between 2020 and 2021, with n equal to ninety-six initially screened, thirty-four excluded for reasons listed, and sixty-two in the final analytic sample with respiratory pathogen testing. 2.3Data collectionDemographic and clinical data were extracted from charts and electronic medical records by trained reviewers. Variables included age, sex, body weight, height, body mass index (BMI), symptom type and duration, oxygen saturation (SpO2), hospital admission/continued inpatient management, intensive care unit (ICU) admission, mechanical ventilation/noninvasive respiratory support, length of hospital and ICU stay, white blood cell count (WBC), C-reactive protein (CRP), procalcitonin, pathogen test results, co-detection, antiviral therapy, antibiotic therapy, corticosteroid use, supportive treatment, severity classification, and clinical outcome. Personal identifiers were coded before analysis. 2.4Pathogen testingRespiratory specimens were tested using real-time fluorescent quantitative PCR (polymerase chain reaction) assays for common respiratory viruses and Mycoplasma pneumoniae RNA/DNA. Nasopharyngeal swab specimens were collected within 24 h of presentation and processed in the hospital's clinical microbiology laboratory using a multiplex respiratory pathogen panel targeting influenza A and B viruses, respiratory syncytial virus, human rhinovirus, human bocavirus, human metapneumovirus, parainfluenza viruses 1–3, adenovirus, seasonal coronaviruses, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Each assay run included a positive control, a negative (no-template) control, and an internal amplification control to monitor extraction and amplification efficiency, following the reagent manufacturer's instructions and routine laboratory quality-assurance procedures. A specimen was classified as positive for a given pathogen when the cycle-threshold value was below the manufacturer-specified cutoff with a typical sigmoidal amplification curve and a valid internal control; results with an invalid internal control or atypical amplification curve were repeated before being reported. 2.5DefinitionsARI was defined clinically by compatible acute respiratory symptoms. Severity was categorized as mild, moderate, or severe. Co-detection was defined as detection of more than one respiratory pathogen in the same illness episode. Clinical outcome was categorized as recovery, complication, or death according to discharge records. Hospital admission/continued inpatient management was defined as continued observation and treatment beyond the initial emergency evaluation, consistent with the emergency-department-based case mix of this cohort, in which most children were evaluated, treated, and discharged without formal ward admission. Mechanical ventilatory/noninvasive respiratory support was recorded independently of formal admission status and could be provided during emergency-department management; therefore, the number of children receiving such support does not necessarily correspond to the number meeting admission criteria. 2.6Ethical considerationsThe study was approved by the Ethics Committee. Because this was a retrospective analysis of de-identified records, the requirement for individual informed consent was waived. 2.7Statistical analysisContinuous variables were summarized using medians and ranges because the distributions were non-normal and the sample was small. Categorical variables were summarized as frequencies and percentages. Sex-based and pathogen-detection group comparisons were performed using Mann–Whitney U tests for continuous variables and Fisher exact or chi-square tests for categorical variables as appropriate. Comparisons across severity categories used Kruskal–Wallis tests with post-hoc pairwise comparisons when the global test was significant. Binary logistic regression was used exploratorily to assess predictors of hospital admission/continued inpatient management. Ordinal logistic regression was used exploratorily for severity. papers.title_original: Clinical characteristics, pathogen detection, and severity markers among children with acute respiratory infections during the COVID-19 restriction period: a retrospective hospital-based study

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the clinical characteristics, pathogen detection, and severity markers of acute respiratory infections (ARIs) in children during the COVID-19 restriction period in China, to better understand the impact of these restrictions on respiratory virus epidemiology and clinical outcomes.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This was a retrospective hospital-based study conducted in China from January 2020 to December 2021, involving 62 children with ARIs who had available pathogen testing results. The study focused on those evaluated during the period of strict public health measures related to the pandemic.
analysis.methods: The study extracted demographic, clinical, laboratory, treatment, severity, and outcome variables from medical records. It applied exclusion criteria to remove duplicate encounters, incomplete records, and cases without respiratory pathogen test results. The study was not powered to detect small effect sizes and used exploratory logistic regression to analyze associations between symptom duration and hospital admission.
analysis.main_results: The median age was 9 years (range, 1–17), and 33 children (53.2%) were female. Fever was the most common presenting symptom (43.5%), followed by cough alone (22.6%), with 19.4% having both fever and cough. Respiratory virus detection was recorded in 15 children (24.2%), with human rhinovirus being the most frequent (24.2%), followed by human bocavirus (14.5%) and Mycoplasma pneumoniae (16.1%). Co-detection was observed in 14 children (22.6%).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that respiratory virus detection was common but varied in frequency, with human rhinovirus being the most frequently detected virus. They noted that Mycoplasma pneumoniae was detected in a smaller but clinically relevant proportion, suggesting its potential role in disease severity.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings provide insights into the epidemiology and clinical manifestations of respiratory viruses in children during the pandemic, which can inform surveillance strategies and public health measures aimed at mitigating the spread of these pathogens.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was limited by its small sample size and sparse severe-outcome events, which reduced its power to detect small effect sizes. The evidence is moderate due to the observational nature of the study and the lack of randomized or controlled components.

analysis.summary_en: This retrospective hospital-based study analyzed clinical characteristics, pathogen detection, and severity markers of acute respiratory infections (ARIs) in 62 children in China during the COVID-19 restriction period. The median age was 9 years, with 53.2% female. Fever was the most common symptom, followed by cough. Respiratory viruses were detected in 24.2% of children, with human rhinovirus being the most frequent. Mycoplasma pneumoniae was detected in 16.1% of cases, and co-detection was observed in 22.6% of children. Most cases were mild, with only 9.7% requiring ICU admission. The study highlights the impact of pandemic restrictions on respiratory virus circulation and clinical outcomes, but its moderate evidence strength is limited by the small sample size and lack of power to detect small effects.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在调查中国COVID-19限制期间儿童急性呼吸道感染(ARIs)的临床特征、病原体检测和严重程度标志物,以更好地了解这些限制对呼吸道病毒流行病学和临床结果的影响。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 这是一项 2020 年 1 月至 2021 年 12 月在中国进行的回顾性医院研究,涉及 62 名具有可用病原体检测结果的 ARI 儿童。该研究的重点是在与大流行相关的严格公共卫生措施期间进行评估的人员。
elements_zh.methods: 该研究从医疗记录中提取了人口统计、临床、实验室、治疗、严重程度和结果变量。它应用排除标准来消除重复遭遇、不完整记录和没有呼吸道病原体检测结果的病例。该研究无法检测小效应大小,并使用探索性逻辑回归来分析症状持续时间与入院之间的关联。
elements_zh.main_results: 中位年龄为 9 岁(范围为 1-17 岁),其中 33 名儿童 (53.2%) 为女性。发烧是最常见的症状(43.5%),其次是咳嗽(22.6%),19.4%的人同时发烧和咳嗽。15名儿童(24.2%)检测到呼吸道病毒,其中最常见的是人鼻病毒(24.2%),其次是人博卡病毒(14.5%)和肺炎支原体(16.1%)。在 14 名儿童(22.6%)中观察到了共同检测。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,呼吸道病毒检测很常见,但频率各不相同,其中人鼻病毒是最常检测到的病毒。他们指出,检测到的肺炎支原体比例较小,但与临床相关,这表明其在疾病严重程度中具有潜在作用。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现提供了对大流行期间儿童呼吸道病毒 流行病学 和临床表现的深入了解,这可以为旨在减轻这些病原体传播的 监测 策略和公共卫生措施提供信息。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究受到样本量小和严重后果事件稀疏的限制,从而降低了检测小效应大小的能力。由于该研究的观察性质以及缺乏随机或对照成分,证据是中等的。

analysis_zh.main_results: 中位年龄为 9 岁(范围为 1-17 岁),其中 33 名儿童 (53.2%) 为女性。发烧是最常见的症状(43.5%),其次是咳嗽(22.6%),19.4%的人同时发烧和咳嗽。15名儿童(24.2%)检测到呼吸道病毒,其中最常见的是人鼻病毒(24.2%),其次是人博卡病毒(14.5%)和肺炎支原体(16.1%)。在 14 名儿童(22.6%)中观察到了共同检测。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,呼吸道病毒检测很常见,但频率各不相同,其中人鼻病毒是最常检测到的病毒。他们指出,检测到的肺炎支原体比例较小,但与临床相关,这表明其在疾病严重程度中具有潜在作用。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现提供了对大流行期间儿童呼吸道病毒 流行病学 和临床表现的深入了解,这可以为旨在减轻这些病原体传播的 监测 策略和公共卫生措施提供信息。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究受到样本量小和严重后果事件稀疏的限制,从而降低了检测小效应大小的能力。由于该研究的观察性质以及缺乏随机或对照成分,证据是中等的。

news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Sunday, October 18, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Human Metapneumovirus Surged in Central China Before Collapsing a Year Later by October 18, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Human Metapneumovirus Surged in Central China Before Collapsing a Year Later Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Human metapneumovirus, a paramyxovirus long overshadowed by influenza and respiratory syncytial virus, staged a dramatic resurgence in central China in late 2024 before its circulation collapsed the following year, according to a large sentinel surveillance study from Henan Province. Researchers at the Henan Provincial Center for Disease Control and Prevention and their collaborators analyzed 36,143 respiratory specimens collected from patients with influenza-like illness or severe acute respiratory infection during 2024 and 2025, screening each sample with multiplex PCR panels covering HMPV and 14 other respiratory pathogens. The results, published in BMC Infectious Diseases, offer one of the most detailed post-pandemic portraits of HMPV epidemiology to date and reveal striking patterns in age distribution, bacterial co-detection, and the temporal choreography between competing respiratory viruses. The headline finding is a sharp inter-year contrast. Overall HMPV positivity across the two-year surveillance period stood at 3.96 percent, with 1,432 of 36,143 specimens testing positive, but that average conceals two very different years. In 2024, 7.1 percent of tested patients carried the virus; in 2025 the figure fell to just 1.7 percent, a more than fourfold decline. The 2024 epidemic peaked with remarkable intensity: during week 48 of that year, 26.2 percent of all tested respiratory specimens were positive for HMPV, a level few endemic respiratory viruses reach even at the height of a seasonal wave. The authors emphasize that the marked resurgence warrants continued monitoring to determine whether such patterns represent a short-term anomaly or a sustained shift in how HMPV circulates in the region. Age played a decisive role in who was infected. Children aged 3 to 5 years recorded the highest positivity of any group, at 8.6 percent, corresponding to an enrichment ratio of 2.18 relative to the overall population under surveillance. The concentration became even more extreme during the peak transmission window: supplementary data show that during weeks 48 to 50 of 2024, HMPV positivity among children aged 3 to 5 climbed to 40.7 percent, meaning that roughly two in five young children tested during that brief period carried detectable virus. Preschool children, it appears, were the engine of the 2024 outbreak, a pattern consistent with HMPV’s biology as a virus that spreads efficiently in settings where young children mix closely and have limited accumulated immunity. Discover more Find Lung Care Check Symptoms Read Med Journals Study Biology Perhaps the most consequential finding concerns what accompanied the virus. Co-infections were detected in 56.2 percent of HMPV-positive cases, and the predominant partners were bacteria rather than other viruses: Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae were the most frequently co-detected organisms. Both are common colonizers of the human nasopharynx that can turn pathogenic when viral infection disrupts mucosal defenses, and their frequent co-detection with HMPV raises questions about the contribution of bacterial carriage to disease severity in pediatric respiratory illness. The study’s statistical framework went beyond simple co-detection rates, quantifying pathogen associations through odds ratios that distinguish genuine ecological interaction from chance overlap in a busy respiratory season. Those odds ratios paint a picture of competitive and facilitative relationships within the respiratory microbiome. HMPV showed a positive association with Streptococcus pneumoniae, with an odds ratio of 2.01, and a weaker positive association with Haemophilus influenzae, at 1.47. Human bocavirus, a virus whose clinical significance remains debated, also tracked positively with HMPV at an odds ratio of 1.66. In contrast, the relationships with the two major winter respiratory viruses were strongly negative: HMPV was negatively associated with influenza virus (odds ratio 0.20) and with respiratory syncytial virus (odds ratio 0.17). Such inverse associations suggest that these viruses do not simply peak independently; each appears to suppress or be suppressed by the others, whether through interference at the host level, depletion of susceptible individuals, or behavioral and environmental factors that favor one agent at a time. Discover more Find Treatments infection Infectious Diseases The temporal analysis added a dynamic dimension to these static associations. Using cross-correlation and regression techniques on weekly surveillance data, the researchers found that respiratory syncytial virus positivity at a one-week lag had a positive effect on subsequent HMPV positivity, with a regression coefficient of 0.15 that reached statistical significance at P equals 0.048. In practical terms, an RSV wave in a given week slightly preceded and predicted a rise in HMPV detections the following week. This lead-lag relationship is intriguing because it coexists with the overall negative association between the two viruses across the full dataset, hinting at a nuanced interaction in which one virus may briefly facilitate conditions for another before competition or immunity-driven exclusion takes over across the longer arc of the season. Methodologically, the study illustrates the value of dense, multiplexed sentinel surveillance. By testing every specimen against 15 pathogens simultaneously, the team could compute enrichment ratios identifying which age groups disproportionately contributed to transmission, pairwise odds ratios revealing pathogen associations, and time-series models capturing the ordering of epidemic waves. The distinction between influenza-like illness and severe acute respiratory infection cases in the sentinel framework also matters, because viruses and co-pathogens may distribute differently across the spectrum of severity. Findings of this kind are difficult to obtain from clinical testing alone, which is typically biased toward severely ill patients and ordered on an ad hoc basis rather than systematically. The public health implications are twofold. First, the high rate of bacterial co-detection argues for integrated surveillance that monitors respiratory bacteria alongside viruses, since pneumococcus and Haemophilus influenzae are both vaccine-preventable in their major serotypes, and their co-circulation with HMPV may shape the clinical burden of an HMPV season. Second, the temporal lead-lag relationship with RSV underscores the authors’ call for integrated pathogen surveillance: signals from one virus’s epidemic curve may serve as early indicators for another, improving the timeliness of clinical preparedness in pediatrics. The strong concentration of cases among children aged 3 to 5 further supports age-targeted prevention strategies, whether through caregiver hygiene measures, cohorting in preschool settings, or, eventually, vaccines and monoclonal approaches now in development for HMPV, which currently has no licensed specific countermeasure. Open questions remain. Henan, a province of nearly 100 million people in central China, provides a robust but geographically specific vantage point, and whether the 2024 surge reflects an immunity debt accrued during pandemic-era contact reductions, viral evolutionary change, or ordinary multi-year epidemic cycling cannot be resolved from two seasons of data. The steep drop in 2025, to 1.7 percent positivity, could indicate that the susceptible pool was largely replenished and depleted within a single intense season, resetting the epidemic clock. The authors themselves frame the 2024 resurgence as a phenomenon requiring continued monitoring, and further seasons of sentinel data will be needed to determine whether HMPV in the region settles into a predictable alternation with RSV and influenza or follows a new post-pandemic rhythm. For now, the study stands as a detailed empirical record of an HMPV outbreak at its peak, capturing a virus that can, in a matter of weeks, infect more than a quarter of young children presenting with acute respiratory illness before receding almost entirely from view. analysis.time: The study analyzed data from 2024 and 2025, with the 2024 epidemic peaking during week 48 of that year. The publication date is October 18, 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The study was conducted in Henan Province, central China, involving 36,143 respiratory specimens collected from patients with influenza-like illness or severe acute respiratory infection.
analysis.event: A large sentinel surveillance study from Henan Province revealed a dramatic resurgence of human metapneumovirus (HMPV) in central China in late 2024, followed by a significant decline in 2025. The study was reported by Bioengineer.org.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Overall HMPV positivity across the two-year surveillance period was 3.96 percent, with 1,432 specimens testing positive. In 2024, positivity reached 7.1 percent, peaking at 26.2 percent during week 48. In 2025, positivity dropped to 1.7 percent. Co-infections were detected in 56.2 percent of HMPV-positive cases, with Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae being the most frequent bacterial partners. The study highlights the need for integrated surveillance and age-targeted prevention strategies.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study emphasizes the need for continued monitoring to determine if the resurgence represents a short-term anomaly or a sustained shift. It also calls for integrated pathogen surveillance and age-targeted prevention strategies. The findings are based on a two-year surveillance period and suggest potential interactions with other respiratory viruses, but the exact mechanisms remain unclear.

analysis.brief_en: A study conducted in Henan Province, central China, revealed a significant surge in human metapneumovirus (HMPV) infections in late 2024, followed by a sharp decline in 2025. Researchers analyzed 36,143 respiratory specimens from patients with influenza-like illness or severe acute respiratory infection, using multiplex PCR panels to detect HMPV alongside 14 other pathogens. The 2024 epidemic peaked at 26.2 percent positivity during week 48, with children aged 3 to 5 years being the most affected, showing an 8.6 percent positivity rate. Co-infections with bacteria like Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae were common, raising concerns about disease severity. The study also found a lead-lag relationship between HMPV and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), suggesting possible interactions. These findings highlight the need for integrated surveillance and age-targeted prevention strategies, as HMPV currently lacks a licensed countermeasure. The authors caution that the observed patterns may reflect immunity debt, viral evolution, or ordinary epidemic cycling, and further research is needed to confirm these possibilities.

news.source_body_en: A study conducted in Henan Province, central China, revealed a significant surge in human metapneumovirus (HMPV) infections in late 2024, followed by a sharp decline in 2025. Researchers analyzed 36,143 respiratory specimens from patients with influenza-like illness or severe acute respiratory infection, using multiplex PCR panels to detect HMPV alongside 14 other pathogens. The 2024 epidemic peaked at 26.2 percent positivity during week 48, with children aged 3 to 5 years being the most affected, showing an 8.6 percent positivity rate. Co-infections with bacteria like Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae were common, raising concerns about disease severity. The study also found a lead-lag relationship between HMPV and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), suggesting possible interactions. These findings highlight the need for integrated surveillance and age-targeted prevention strategies, as HMPV currently lacks a licensed countermeasure. The authors caution that the observed patterns may reflect immunity debt, viral evolution, or ordinary epidemic cycling, and further research is needed to confirm these possibilities.

A new seroepidemiological study conducted in Taizhou city, in eastern China’s Zhejiang Province, now offers one of the most detailed pictures yet of how immunity to this virus is distributed across the human lifespan in the post-pandemic era. The findings, published in BMC Infectious Diseases, reveal a striking vulnerability window in toddlers and suggest that population-level immunity against the virus follows a distinctive age-related trajectory with important implications for future vaccine and prevention strategies. The research team, led by Chang Liu and Qiang Wang of the Shanghai Institute of Infectious Disease and Biosecurity at Fudan University, together with David Hodgson of Charité Universitätsmedizin Berlin and collaborators at the Taizhou City Center for Disease Control and Prevention and the University of Hong Kong, analyzed serum samples collected between June 2 and June 30, 2024. The samples came from a community-based cross-sectional survey that used a multistage, age-stratified sampling design, with deliberate oversampling of children under five years of age to ensure that the youngest and most epidemiologically critical age groups were adequately represented. In total, 1,303 participants aged between 16 months and 93 years were included in the analysis. Discover more Infectious Disease infection Track Biotech Rather than simply measuring whether people had ever been exposed to the virus, the researchers focused on neutralizing antibodies, the subset of antibodies capable of directly blocking viral infection of cells. These were quantified using a fluorescence-based microneutralization assay, a laboratory technique in which serum is serially diluted and mixed with live virus before being applied to cell cultures; the presence of neutralizing activity is then detected through fluorescence-based readouts. A participant was classified as seropositive if their serum neutralized the virus at a dilution of 1:30 or greater. This approach provides a more functionally meaningful measure of protective immunity than binding-antibody tests alone, because neutralization titers correlate more closely with resistance to infection. Check Symptoms Discover more Find Lung Care Read Med Journals Study Biology COVID The central finding concerns children aged 16 to less than 36 months, who displayed the lowest antibody levels of any age group examined. Their geometric mean titer, a standard way of averaging antibody concentrations that are log-distributed across a population, stood at just 217, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 159 to 295. Only 67.8 percent of participants in this age band, 137 out of 202 children tested, were seropositive at all. In practical terms, roughly one in three toddlers in their second and third years of life lacked detectable neutralizing immunity against a virus that commonly causes bronchiolitis and pneumonia in early childhood. Study Biology The picture changes rapidly with age. Among children aged three to four years, the geometric mean titer rose to 331, and by ages five to eleven it exceeded 1,000, a level that was then maintained throughout adulthood. The oldest participants showed the strongest responses of all: adults aged 65 years and older had a geometric mean titer of 1,829, with a confidence interval of 1,620 to 2,064. From the age of six onward, seroprevalence was close to or had reached 100 percent, indicating that nearly everyone in the population had accumulated neutralizing antibodies by school age, most likely through repeated natural infections during early childhood. Within the under-five group, the age gradient was particularly steep. The researchers calculated that for each additional year of age, neutralizing antibody titers increased by 74.7 percent, with a 95 percent confidence interval ranging from 14.4 percent to 167.0 percent. This rapid accumulation of immunity in the first years of life is consistent with the known epidemiology of human metapneumovirus, which circulates seasonally and infects a large proportion of children before their fifth birthday. The low titers observed in the 16-to-36-month window likely reflect the combination of waning maternal antibodies, limited cumulative exposure, and the immature antibody responses characteristic of early childhood. The timing of the study adds a layer of epidemiological significance. The COVID-19 pandemic and the non-pharmaceutical interventions that accompanied it, including masking, school closures, and physical distancing, dramatically suppressed transmission of many respiratory pathogens worldwide, and human metapneumovirus was no exception. When these measures were relaxed, several respiratory viruses returned with unusual intensity and atypical seasonality, raising concerns about whether cohorts of children who grew up during the interruption had missed their usual early exposures and were now entering a period of heightened susceptibility. The Taizhou data suggest that by mid-2024, transmission had resumed sufficiently to rebuild immunity in older children, but that toddlers remained a partially unprotected reservoir of susceptibility. Read Med Journals Discover more Check Symptoms COVID-19 Get Rapid Tests Read Health News Infectious Diseases One of the more intriguing aspects of the study is its exploration of the relationship between immunity to human metapneumovirus and respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, a closely related paramyxovirus. The researchers measured IgG antibodies against the prefusion F protein of RSV, the key surface protein targeted by protective antibodies, and examined how these correlated with metapneumovirus neutralization titers. They found a statistically significant positive association: higher RSV prefusion F IgG titers were linked to higher metapneumovirus neutralizing titers, with a Spearman correlation coefficient of 0.302 and a p-value below 0.001. The authors are careful to note that this correlation does not prove a causal mechanism. It may reflect shared epidemiological exposures, since both viruses circulate in overlapping seasonal windows and spread through similar routes, meaning that individuals with more respiratory virus exposure in general would tend to have higher titers against both. Individual differences in the vigor of immune responses could also produce the same pattern, with some people mounting stronger antibody responses to any viral challenge. A third possibility is genuine cross-reactive immunity, in which antibodies raised against one virus recognize structurally similar proteins on the other, a phenomenon documented for other paramyxoviruses. Distinguishing among these explanations will require longitudinal studies and laboratory work with cross-neutralization assays. The practical implications of the study are considerable. No licensed vaccine or prophylactic product currently exists for human metapneumovirus, although several vaccine candidates are in development, and monoclonal antibodies and maternal immunization strategies are being explored for RSV, raising the prospect of similar approaches for its viral cousin. In the absence of immunization tools, the identification of children aged 16 to 36 months as the group with the lowest seroprevalence and weakest titers provides a clear target for surveillance and, eventually, for preventive interventions. The authors emphasize that continued monitoring of this age group is essential, both to track how post-pandemic transmission dynamics reshape the immunity landscape and to inform the design and prioritization of future vaccination programs. As the global health community absorbs the lesson that pandemic-era disruptions can leave lasting imprints on the epidemiology of common respiratory viruses, studies like this one demonstrate the value of population-based serosurveillance in pinpointing exactly where those imprints fall and who remains most at risk. The Taizhou data suggest that by mid-2024, transmission had resumed sufficiently to rebuild immunity in older children, but that toddlers remained a partially unprotected reservoir of susceptibility. Read Med Journals Discover more Check Symptoms COVID-19 Get Rapid Tests Read Health News Infectious Diseases One of the more intriguing aspects of the study is its exploration of the relationship between immunity to human metapneumovirus and respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, a closely related paramyxovirus. The researchers measured IgG antibodies against the prefusion F protein of RSV, the key surface protein targeted by protective antibodies, and examined how these correlated with metapneumovirus neutralization titers. They found a statistically significant positive association: higher RSV prefusion F IgG titers were linked to higher metapneumovirus neutralizing titers, with a Spearman correlation coefficient of 0.302 and a p-value below 0.001. The authors are careful to note that this correlation does not prove a causal mechanism. It may reflect shared epidemiological exposures, since both viruses circulate in overlapping seasonal windows and spread through similar routes, meaning that individuals with more respiratory virus exposure in general would tend to have higher titers against both. Individual differences in the vigor of immune responses could also produce the same pattern, with some people mounting stronger antibody responses to any viral challenge. A third possibility is genuine cross-reactive immunity, in which antibodies raised against one virus recognize structurally similar proteins on the other, a phenomenon documented for other paramyxoviruses. Distinguishing among these explanations will require longitudinal studies and laboratory work with cross-neutralization assays. The practical implications of the study are considerable. No licensed vaccine or prophylactic product currently exists for human metapneumovirus, although several vaccine candidates are in development, and monoclonal antibodies and maternal immunization strategies are being explored for RSV, raising the prospect of similar approaches for its viral cousin. In the absence of immunization tools, the identification of children aged 16 to 36 months as the group with the lowest seroprevalence and weakest titers provides a clear target for surveillance and, eventually, for preventive interventions. The authors emphasize that continued monitoring of this age group is essential, both to track how post-pandemic transmission dynamics reshape the immunity landscape and to inform the design and prioritization of future vaccination programs. As the global health community absorbs the lesson that pandemic-era disruptions can leave lasting imprints on the epidemiology of common respiratory viruses, studies like this one demonstrate the value of population-based serosurveillance in pinpointing exactly where those imprints fall and who remains most at risk.
